Boleno & Newcombe

30 Oct 2026Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 1 Appellate)[2026] FedCFamC1A 191Migration: court challengeMigration
This was an appeal by a father against final parenting orders requiring his time with the child to be professionally supervised until she turns 10, after the primary judge found he posed an unacceptable risk of psychological harm. The appellate court dismissed the appeal, holding that no relevant error was established, and made costs orders against the appellant.
Key holding

In determining whether a parent poses an unacceptable risk of future harm, a court may rely on findings about past conduct and present insight as the foundation for the predictive assessment.

Furthermore, the predictive exercise of risk assessment cannot be undertaken other than by reference to past events.

FDB17 v Minister for Immigration, Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs

29 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1612Migration: court challengeMigration
The appellant, a Pakistani protection visa applicant, appealed a Federal Circuit and Family Court judgment dismissing his judicial review application concerning an AAT decision that affirmed refusal of his visa. He argued the Tribunal fell into jurisdictional error by unreasonably declining to telephone four corroborating witnesses (his parents, brother and a friend) who had already provided a joint signed statement. The Federal Court dismissed the appeal, holding the Tribunal's approach had a rational and intelligible foundation.
Key holding

Where a decision-maker is convinced that an applicant's account is fabricated or fundamentally unreliable, it is not irrational or illogical to decline to hear oral corroborating evidence and to reject that corroboration, even absent any independent ground for doubting the corroborators.

It is not necessarily irrational, or illogical, for a finder of fact, who is convinced that a principal witness is fabricating a story, which is considered to be inherently implausible, to reject corroborative evidence, even though there is no separate or independent ground for its rejection, apart from the reasons given for disbelieving the principal witness.

Rangel & Bird (No 2)

29 Oct 2026Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 1 Appellate)[2026] FedCFamC1A 193Migration: court challengeMigration
This was a mother’s appeal against three parenting orders concerning the children’s international travel, passports and extra-curricular activities. The appellate court found the primary judge denied procedural fairness by making orders materially outside the case presented by the parties and the Independent Children’s Lawyer. The appeal was allowed, the relevant orders were set aside, and the discretion was re-exercised.
Key holding

Procedural fairness ordinarily requires that parties be given an opportunity to address an order materially outside the range of orders sought or reasonably anticipated, and breach is appealable where material.

While a primary judge is not bound by the parties' and the ICL's proposals ( U v U [2002] HCA 36 ; (2002) 211 CLR 238) , procedural fairness ordinarily requires that the parties be afforded an opportunity to address a course materially outside the range of orders sought or reasonably anticipated ( Duarte & Morse [2019] FamCAFC 93 ; (2019) FLC 93-902).

Jamdar v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

28 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1620Migration: court challengeMigration
The Federal Court granted an extension of time but dismissed an appeal from the Administrative Review Tribunal, which had affirmed refusal of Australian citizenship by conferral on good-character grounds. The applicant challenged the Tribunal’s treatment of earlier non-conviction offending and its finding that he deliberately withheld his 2023 conviction.
Key holding

Part VIIC of the Crimes Act 1914 (Cth) precludes reliance on the fact of a charge, conviction or finding of guilt, but does not preclude an administrative decision-maker from considering the underlying conduct.

Sections 85ZR and 85ZS are directed to the fact of a charge, conviction or finding of guilt and do not expressly preclude an administrative decision-maker from considering the underlying conduct.

Kearney v Migration Agents Registration Authority

28 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1615Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationMigration
This was an appeal to the Federal Court from a Tribunal decision affirming cancellation of a migration agent’s registration for five years under s 303(1)(a) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal found the agent breached the Code of Conduct and was not a fit and proper person, based on nomination applications lodged for nine businesses without their knowledge or permission. Dowling J dismissed the appeal.
Key holding

Under the former reg 3(1) definition, a migration agent’s client includes any person to whom the agent agrees to provide immigration assistance, even without a retainer or the person’s express or implied acceptance.

I agree with the Authority's submissions and accept that 'client', as it was defined by reg 3(1) of the Regulations at the time of the applicant's conduct in question, includes persons to whom a registered migration agent agrees to provide immigration assistance even in the absence of a retainer or where the recipient of the assistance has not expressly or impliedly agreed to receive it.

ZKDP and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration)

27 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2505Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewCharacter testMigration
ZKDP sought review of a delegate’s refusal to revoke the mandatory cancellation of his visa after a 7-year-6-month drug trafficking sentence. The Tribunal found he did not pass the character test but nevertheless set aside the refusal and substituted revocation after applying Direction No. 110. It weighed community protection against ties, rehabilitation, pending charges and other factors in a fact-specific decision.
Key holding

Under s 501CA(4) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth), a mandatory cancellation may be revoked where the required representations have been made and the decision-maker is satisfied that there is another reason why the original decision should be revoked.

Under s 501CA(4) of the Act, the Minister may revoke the original decision to cancel if the person makes representations in accordance with the invitation and the Minister is satisfied that the person passes the character test or there is another reason why the original decision should be revoked.

Yang and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Citizenship)

27 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2501Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewCharacter testMigration
This was a review of a delegate’s refusal to approve Australian citizenship by descent under s 17(1A) of the Australian Citizenship Act 2007 (Cth), because the delegate was not satisfied the applicant had an Australian citizen parent at the time of her birth under s 16(2)(a). The Tribunal affirmed the refusal after finding the documentary evidence unreliable or insufficient and the claimed parent-child relationship with Mr Yang not established at birth.
Key holding

For the purposes of s 16(2)(a) of the Citizenship Act, a claimed parent-child relationship, whether biological or non-biological, must be shown to have existed at the time of the child’s birth and cannot be established by a later relationship.

Hence, in considering whether the Applicant may be the non-biological child of an Australian citizen parent, the relationship must have existed at the time of the birth of the child. The relationship cannot be developed at a later stage.

Fred-Tutavaha v Assistant Minister for Citizenship, Customs and Multicultural Affairs

26 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1586Migration: court challengeMigration
The applicant, a New Zealand citizen who arrived in Australia aged four, sought judicial review of the Assistant Minister's decision under s 501BA of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to set aside an AAT decision revoking the cancellation of his visa. He ran three grounds — unreasonable delay, failure to consider immigration detention as a legal consequence, and legal unreasonableness in giving legal consequences "neutral weight" — with the Court also considering a proposed fourth ground on the national interest assessment.
Key holding

A failure to refer expressly to immigration detention in reasons for a s 501BA cancellation does not permit an inference that this legal consequence was not considered, where detention pending removal is an obvious and well-known statutory consequence and there is no barrier to removal.

It does not follow, however, that the proper inference is that the Assistant Minister failed to appreciate that a legal consequence of his decision was that the Applicant would be taken into immigration detention. The statement of reasons must be read fairly and as a whole, and the fact that a matter is not mentioned expressly does not necessarily mean it was not considered

Fotu v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

23 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1589Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationMigration
The Federal Court set aside the Assistant Minister’s personal decision under s 501BA(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to override an Administrative Review Tribunal decision and cancel Mr Fotu’s visa. Harvey v State of Queensland

23 Oct 2026Queensland Court of Appeal[2026] QCA 214Migration: court challengeMigration
The Queensland Court of Appeal dismissed Mr Harvey’s appeal from a decision refusing to set aside his notice of discontinuance of a police assault damages claim filed more than seven years earlier. The Court found no error in the primary judge’s discretionary conclusion that the appellant had not shown good reason, or that the interests of justice required, setting aside the discontinuance, given unparticularised evidence and unexplained delay.
Key holding

Even if a court may set aside a notice of discontinuance where the interests of justice require it, unparticularised claims of duress or mental illness and lengthy unexplained delay will not satisfy that test.

Assuming in the appellant's favour that the court had power to set aside the discontinuance if it was shown to be in the interests of justice to do so, the material before the primary judge did not satisfy that test.

Darlington-Thomas v Elgas Limited

21 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1566Migration: court challengeMigration
The Federal Court granted Ms Darlington-Thomas leave under s 46PO(3A)(a) of the Australian Human Rights Commission Act 1986 (Cth) to proceed against her labour hire employer, Zoom, for alleged disability discrimination. The AHRC had terminated her complaint against Zoom, but the Court held the claim was reasonably arguable and should be resolved with the overlapping claim against Elgas.
Key holding

On an application for leave under s 46PO(3A)(a) of the AHRC Act, the Court asks only whether the proposed discrimination claim is reasonably arguable and not fanciful, rather than determining the merits.

I am satisfied that the text, context and purpose of the leave requirement in s 46PO(3A) suggests that it is appropriate for the Court to consider in determining whether to grant leave whether the claims made by an applicant are reasonably arguable, and are - at the least - not fanciful. This is consistent with the language used in s 46P(1A).

Gibson and Chief Executive Officer, National Disability Insurance Agency (Practice and procedure)

20 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2437Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
The Tribunal refused an application to appoint NDIS participant Shannon Gibson’s support coordinator, Geeta Carroll, as his litigation supporter in a Tribunal review about his NDIS plan. Although the Tribunal accepted that Mr Gibson lacked decision-making ability, it was not satisfied that the appointment was “necessary” because his representative, plan-nominee mother, interpreter, Tribunal adjustments and informal supports already allowed participation.
Key holding

Under s 67(1)(b) of the Administrative Review Tribunal Act 2024 (Cth), a litigation supporter is not “necessary” merely because appointment is desirable, expedient, convenient or preferable; it is a last-resort measure required only where available and suitable other measures do not allow the party to participate.

It follows that the use of the word necessary has the effect that an appointment that would make the proceeding easier or more convenient to manage, or that the parties would welcome, is not for that reason 'necessary'. The choice of the word emphasises that an appointment is a measure of last resort, made only where the party cannot otherwise participate.

Lippl and CEO, National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIS)

This NDIS review concerned whether Ms Lippl should receive additional 1:1 support worker hours beyond those in her statement of participant supports. Additional requested NDIS support worker hours are not reasonable and necessary where the evidence shows the participant can use current flexible funding to meet needs and increased hours risk dependency, so the value-for-money criterion is not met.

BNE24 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

20 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1561Migration: court challengeMigration
This was an appeal from the Federal Circuit and Family Court (Division 2) dismissing review of a Tribunal decision refusing a protection visa. The unrepresented appellant argued the Tribunal’s adverse credibility findings were illogical or unreasonable. The Federal Court dismissed the appeal, holding the primary judge correctly found no jurisdictional error.
Key holding

A Tribunal’s adverse credibility finding does not involve jurisdictional error merely because a reviewing court would have reached a different factual finding; the reasoning must be legally unreasonable.

Therefore, jurisdictional error in the reasoning by the Tribunal as to the credibility of the account given by an applicant is not established by seeking to persuade a court on review that the Tribunal's reasoning includes an error in the sense that the Court would not make the same finding.

Australian Securities and Investments Commission v Dawson

20 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1548Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewCharacter testMigration
SXHR, a Sri Lankan unauthorised maritime arrival in immigration detention, sought judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Bridging E visa under s 501(1) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal had applied Direction No 110 and refused the visa notwithstanding the applicant’s outstanding Ministerial intervention request. The Federal Court dismissed the review.

Macrolend Pty Ltd v Deputy Commissioner of Taxation

25 Sep 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1501Migration: court challengeMigration
Macrolend Pty Ltd and Paladin Hydrogen Pty Ltd sought recusal of Derrington J from their applications to set aside Deputy Commissioner of Taxation statutory demands, alleging apprehended bias because his spouse, Sarah C Derrington J, had previously made overlapping findings in related ASIC proceedings. Derrington J dismissed the recusal application, finding no reasonable apprehension of bias. The plaintiffs were ordered to pay the defendant’s costs and the substantive matter was listed for hearing on 2 October 2026.
Key holding

A judge is not required to recuse for apprehended bias merely because their spouse has previously made overlapping findings of fact or credit in related proceedings; there must be a rational logical connection between that relationship or those findings and a possible departure from impartial merits-based decision-making.

Nor would my relationship with Sarah C Derrington J provide such a basis. There is no rational reason to apprehend that, because of that relationship, I might adopt her Honour's findings, depart from them to demonstrate my independence, or resolve the issues otherwise than on their legal and factual merits.

Burgess & Burgess (No 2)

23 Sep 2026Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 1 First Instance)[2026] FedCFamC1F 649Migration: court challengeMigration
This was a part-heard family law property proceeding under s 79 of the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) in which the wife sought to rely on a covert audio recording of the husband. After the High Court’s decision in Potter (A Pseudonym) v The King [2026] HCA 25, Parker J revisited an earlier interlocutory ruling admitting the recording, excluded it, recused herself, and aborted the trial. The husband was granted a costs certificate.
Key holding

In South Australia, s 9(1) of the Surveillance Devices Act 2016 (SA) (and by parity s 12(1)) is a law relating to evidence picked up by s 79(1) of the Judiciary Act and applies in federal family law proceedings, so a recording obtained for a lawful-interest purpose cannot be used unless a s 9(1) exception applies, and s 138 of the Evidence Act does not displace that prohibition.

In my view, subsection 9(1) is therefore a "law relating to evidence," the effect of which is that it is "picked up" by section 79 of the Judiciary Act[17] such that the same limitation applies in the context of a court exercising federal jurisdiction in South Australia, as is the case in the present proceeding. The same reasoning applies with respect to subsection 12(1) of the Surveillance Devices Act.

Asad v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

27 Aug 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1477Migration: court challengeMigration
Mr Asad sought an extension of time to judicially review the Assistant Minister’s decision under s 501BA of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to set aside the Tribunal’s decision and cancel his resident return visa. As a member of the NZYQ cohort, Mr Asad would remain in the community even if the visa were cancelled. The Federal Court granted an extension only for part of ground 1 but dismissed the application, finding the cancellation decision was not illogical or irrational.
Key holding

In assessing the national interest under s 501BA, it is not illogical or irrational to cancel a visa on protection-of-the-community grounds where the decision-maker distinguishes the permanent risk of continued residence on a substantive visa from the non-permanent, even if indefinite, risk on a temporary or bridging visa.

The former necessarily created a permanent risk, while the latter created a risk that had at least the potential or possibility to be non-permanent, even if of indefinite duration at the time the decision was made.

Determining whether a position is genuine under reg 2.72(10)(a) requires a qualitative assessment comparing the position with the nominated occupation.

In 2104609 (Refugee) [2026] ARTA 2306, the Tribunal reviewed a delegate’s refusal of protection visas to Indian nationals in an interfaith/inter-caste marriage who claimed family and honour-based violence in Punjab. Key holding

A protection visa may be granted on complementary protection grounds where the refugee criterion is not met, if removal creates a real risk of significant harm as a necessary and foreseeable consequence.

The issues in this case are whether the applicants have a well-founded fear of being persecuted in India for one or more of the five reasons set out, and, if not, whether there are substantial grounds for believing that, as a necessary and foreseeable consequence of the applicant being removed from Australia to India there is a real risk that they will suffer significant harm.

For Commonwealth offences, the common law requirement that hardship to family be "exceptional" before it significantly mitigates sentence does not apply, because s 16A(2)(p) of the Crimes Act 1914 (Cth) directs the court to take into account the probable effect of the sentence on family or dependants according to its terms.

However, it has been clear in this state since the decision in Totaan [2022] NSWCCA 75, that this is not so in cases involving Commonwealth offences. Mdallal (Migration)

18 May 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2382Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationMigration
This was a review of a delegate’s decision to cancel Mr Mdallal’s Subclass 820 (Spouse) visa after he was convicted of contravening an AVO and common assault. Although the Tribunal found the conviction ground for cancellation was made out, it exercised the discretion not to cancel because of his remarriage, his support for two minor children (including an autistic stepdaughter), and the hardship removal would cause. The Tribunal set aside the cancellation and substituted a decision not to cancel.
Key holding

Even where a conviction ground for cancellation under s 116(1)(g) is established, the Tribunal may decline to cancel a temporary spouse visa where the best interests of affected children and associated family hardship outweigh the seriousness of the offending in the particular circumstances.

In the particular circumstances of this case, the Tribunal has decided to give greatest weight to the best interests of the children which weigh against the cancellation. Considering the circumstances as a whole, the Tribunal concludes that the cancellation should be set aside.

Mr Sharma sought a Regional Sponsored Migration Scheme (subclass 187) visa based on a nomination by Shivram Australia Pty Ltd. 2114521 (Refugee)

16 Sep 2025Administrative Review Tribunal[2025] ARTA 3466Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
The Tribunal reviewed a delegate’s refusal of a subclass 866 protection visa to a Chinese national who claimed persecution arising from a family shop/land dispute involving local government, a developer and his father’s petitioning. At hearing, the applicant contradicted those written claims, said he did not fear harm on return to China, and explained he wished to stay in Australia for work and family financial reasons. Key holding

An applicant for a protection visa bears the responsibility to establish all statutory elements by sufficient evidence, and the Tribunal is not required to make the applicant’s case.

It remains for the applicant to satisfy the Tribunal that all of the statutory elements are established. A decision-maker is not required to make the applicant's case for him or her.

2002567 (Refugee)

11 Oct 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 4218Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Don Smyth
This was an AATA review of a delegate’s refusal of a protection visa to an applicant who claimed South African citizenship but was born and lived in Zimbabwe. He claimed fear in South Africa and/or Zimbabwe as a gay, mixed-race/“coloured” man, a political opponent of Zanu-PF, and because of economic conditions and crime. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal.
Key holding

For complementary protection, a real risk is not established where the risk is one faced by the population generally and not personally by the applicant.

Under s 36(2B)(c) of the Act there is taken not to be a real risk that an applicant will suffer significant harm if the Tribunal is satisfied that the real risk is one faced by the population generally and is not faced by the applicant personally.

2016849 (Refugee)

11 Oct 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 4209Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Lilly Mojsin
This was an Administrative Review Tribunal (Migration & Refugee Division) review of a delegate’s refusal to grant protection visas to Chinese applicants who claimed harm from loan sharks, debt collectors, gangdom and police in China. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal because the applicants consented to a decision on the papers and the Tribunal was not satisfied their claims were made out or that they faced a real chance or real risk of harm on return to China.
Key holding

A protection visa applicant bears the onus of establishing all statutory elements; mere assertions of feared persecution or significant harm are insufficient unless they satisfy the Tribunal that a well-founded fear or real risk exists.

The mere fact that a person claims fear of persecution for a particular reason does not establish either the genuineness of the asserted fear or that it is "well-founded" or that it is for the reason claimed. Similarly, that the applicant claims to face a real risk of significant harm does not establish that such a risk exists, or that the harm feared amounts to "significant harm".

10 Oct 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 4472Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Rupert Timms
The Tribunal reviewed a delegate’s refusal of a protection visa to a Vietnamese Kinh Buddhist man who claimed fear of harm in Vietnam arising from low-level protest activity in Australia. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal because the evidence did not establish a well-founded fear of persecution or a real risk of significant harm. Key holding

Conduct engaged in by a protection visa applicant in Australia must be disregarded in assessing well-founded fear unless the applicant proves it was not done to strengthen the refugee claim.

In determining whether the person has a well‑founded fear of persecution for one or more of the reasons mentioned in paragraph (1)(a), any conduct engaged in by the person in Australia is to be disregarded unless the person satisfies the Minister that the person engaged in the conduct otherwise than for the purpose of strengthening the person's claim to be a refugee.

1917587 (Refugee)

10 Oct 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 4461Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Frank Russo
The Tribunal reviewed a refusal of protection visas for a Thai family who claimed they feared harm in Thailand from a money lender associated with organised crime over unpaid agricultural debts. The Tribunal accepted the applicants’ identity and nationality but made adverse credibility findings and found no well-founded fear of persecution or real risk of significant harm. It affirmed the delegate’s refusal.
Key holding

A claimed fear of persecution is not well-founded unless supported by credible, non-speculative evidence; the Tribunal may reject uncritical assertions and find the claimed fear not established.

The Tribunal notes that the mere fact that a person claims fear of persecution for a particular reason does not establish the genuineness of the asserted fear, that the fear is "well-founded" or that it is for the reason claimed. A fear of persecution is not "well-founded" if it is merely assumed or if it is mere speculation.

Before: Khanh Hoang

Key holding

In a protection visa review, the applicant bears the responsibility to specify all particulars and provide sufficient evidence, and the Tribunal is not obliged to make the applicant’s case.

It is the responsibility of the applicant to specify all particulars of the claim to be a person in respect of whom Australia has protection obligations and to provide sufficient evidence to establish the claim. The Tribunal does not have any responsibility or obligation to specify, or assist in specifying any particulars of the claim, or to establish or assist in establishing the claim: s 5AAA.

SRFX and Minister for Immigration, Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs (Citizenship)

8 Oct 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3549Tribunal reviewVisa integrityVisa refusal reviewCharacter testMigration
SRFX applied for Australian citizenship by conferral, but a delegate refused approval under s 24(1) of the Australian Citizenship Act 2007 (Cth), finding he did not satisfy the good character requirement in s 21(2)(h) and that his identity could not be established under s 24(3). The Tribunal reviewed the decision, relying on the applicant’s migration history, prior partner visa findings and allegedly bogus documents, and affirmed the refusal. The case turns on whether the Tribunal could be satisfied of his good character and identity.
Key holding

In assessing good character for citizenship, the decision-maker must make a holistic assessment of the person’s enduring moral qualities, and a single sufficiently serious adverse incident can outweigh otherwise good qualities.

The decision-maker must look holistically at applicant's behaviour over time and reach a conclusion about the person's enduring moral qualities. Notwithstanding the obligation to take a holistic approach, it is established that a single adverse incident of sufficient weight and seriousness can outweigh many good qualities in a person.

Key holding

Once the Tribunal has validly reviewed a reviewable decision and completed its statutory review, that decision ceases to be reviewable and the Tribunal lacks jurisdiction to review the same delegate decision again.

Mrs Singh, a 72-year-old New Zealand citizen, applied for Australian citizenship by conferral but had been an Australian permanent resident for less than the 12 months required before her application. The Tribunal affirmed the delegate’s refusal because she did not satisfy the residence requirement and no statutory discretion applied.
Key holding

Eligibility under s 21(3)(c) requires satisfaction of the applicable residence or defence service requirement at the time of application, and the Tribunal cannot waive that requirement through a general discretion absent the statutory conditions.

However, these are not factors that assist Mrs Singh in meeting the residence requirements, or that allow them to be waived. Mrs Singh did not satisfy the general residence requirement (see section 22) or the special residence requirement (see section 22A or 22B), or the defence service requirement (see section 23), at the time she applied for citizenship, and so she does not meet the eligibility requirement of subsection 21(3) of the Citizenship Act.

Dumbaya (Migration)

25 Sep 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3844Tribunal reviewVisa integrityVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Peter Emmerton
This was a review of a delegate’s refusal of a Child (Migrant) (Class AH) visa for Mr Eddie Sheka Sidique. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal.
Key holding

PIC 4020(1) is engaged by a bogus document or false or misleading material information where some person has engaged in fraud or deception, even if the applicant did not know the information was untrue.

While PIC 4020 refers to information that is false, in the sense of purposely untrue, it is not necessary for the Minister (or the Tribunal on review) to conclude that the applicant was aware the information was purposely untrue in order for PIC 4020 to be engaged. However, an element of fraud or deception by some person is necessary to attract the operation of the provision: Trivedi v MIBP [2014] FCAFC 42.

2115044 (Refugee)

24 Sep 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3976Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Sue Zelinka
The applicant, a Macedonian citizen, sought review of a refusal of a protection visa based on feared harm from family and an alleged criminal gang after his secret marriage to his first cousin became known. The Tribunal accepted the marriage and societal stigma but found no real chance of serious harm, given the divorce, his father’s reconciliation, his second marriage, and that “Komiti” was a football supporters’ club. It affirmed the refusal.
Key holding

A particular social group claim cannot succeed where the asserted group is not cognisable because its defining marriage is unlawful in the receiving country, or where the group is defined only by a shared fear of persecution or family harm.

The Tribunal rejects this formulation noting that there is no such group because first cousins, by law, cannot marry in Macedonia and therefore there cannot be a large, cognisable group of them. Any other variation of particular social group involving victims of harm at family hands is also rejected because a particular social group cannot be constituted by persons bound only by fear of persecution.

Before: Paul Windsor
Mr Cai applied for a Visitor (Class FA) subclass 600 visa in the Tourist stream. The delegate refused the visa because it was not satisfied he genuinely intended to stay temporarily in Australia under cl 600.211. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal, finding his long continuous stay and unsupported medical claims indicated he was using the visitor visa to establish de facto residence.
Key holding

To satisfy cl 600.211, the applicant must positively satisfy the Tribunal of a genuine intention to stay temporarily for the visa purpose; a long continuous stay without a credible departure timeframe or supporting medical evidence can show the visitor visa is being used for de facto residence.

A student visa holder’s failure to maintain enrolment in a full-time registered course breaches condition 8202 and enlivens the s 116(1)(b) cancellation ground, after which cancellation is a discretionary decision.

The issue in this case is whether the applicant, as the holder of a student visa, has breached condition 8202 of the Regulations. If so, the ground for cancellation is made out and the issue then becomes whether the visa should be cancelled pursuant to section 116(1) of the Act.

Hughes and Minister for Immigration, Citizenship, and Multicultural Affairs (Migration)

4 Sep 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3158Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa refusal reviewCharacter testMigration
Michael Hughes, a 58-year-old New Zealand/United Kingdom citizen, had his subclass 189 visa mandatorily cancelled after being convicted of indecent dealing with a child under 13 and sentenced to 20 months’ imprisonment. Key holding

In a s 501CA review, the Tribunal cannot go behind the essential facts of the conviction and sentence that founded the mandatory cancellation, and an applicant bears a heavy onus to challenge those facts.

In those circumstances, it is not open to the Tribunal to go behind the essential facts of that conviction and sentence. Moreover, the Applicant has not discharged what would otherwise be his "heavy onus" to challenge the facts upon which the conviction and sentence are necessarily based as set out above.

As the applicant did not apply for reinstatement of the application within the 14 days period, the Tribunal must confirm the decision to dismiss the application. In these circumstances, the decision under review is taken to be affirmed.

Goncalves De Sa (Migration)

28 Aug 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3350Tribunal reviewVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewCharacter testMigration
Before: Peter Emmerton
The Tribunal affirmed refusal of Employer Nomination (Permanent) (Class EN) Subclass 186 visas in the Temporary Residence Transition stream because the primary applicant, a chef, could not demonstrate competent English at the time of application. Although he spoke English well at hearing and had substantial culinary experience, his IELTS results and Portuguese passport did not meet the prescribed criteria, and the Tribunal had no discretion.
Key holding

For a Subclass 186 TRT visa, competent English must be established at the time of application through a specified test score or specified passport, failing which cl 186.222(a) is not satisfied and the Tribunal has no discretion.

Since neither 1.15C(1) nor 1.15C(2) are satisfied, 1.15C is not satisfied. As 1.15C is not satisfied, the Tribunal finds the applicant did not have competent English at the time of lodging the visa application, and therefore does not satisfy 186.222(a).

Jiang (Migration)

28 Aug 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3198Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Tania Flood
The Tribunal affirmed refusal of Ms Jiang’s Visitor (Class FA) Subclass 600 visa because she applied after her substantive visa expired. It found the late application resulted from forgetfulness and inadequate reminders, not factors beyond her control under Schedule 3 criterion 3004(c). The applicant was also offshore at the time of decision, so cl 600.411 was not met.
Key holding

Under criterion 3004(c), whether the applicant ceased to hold a substantive visa because of factors beyond their control is assessed subjectively and practically, and forgetfulness or failure to take available compliance measures will not ordinarily qualify.

The test is in that sense "subjective" rather than being directed at deciding what would have been beyond the control of an abstract or "reasonable" person. A second point is that what is "beyond control" should be tested by considering whether the happening of the event was or was not within the control of the applicant in a practical or realistic sense.

2411742 (Refugee)

27 Aug 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 4375Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa refusal reviewVisa integrityMigration
Before: Damian Creedon
The applicant is an older South Korean citizen who claimed protection in Australia because he feared being unable to find work in South Korea due to age discrimination and long absence. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal of his protection visa, finding South Korea offers effective protection against age discrimination and that his economic/employment concerns did not meet protection criteria.
Key holding

Effective protection measures available from the receiving State can negate a well-founded fear of persecution under s 5J(2).

The Tribunal finds, therefore, that South Korea can offer effective protection to its citizens against age discrimination. It follows, and the Tribunal finds, that effective protection measures against age discrimination are available to the applicant in South Korea, and that therefore he does not have a well-founded fear of persecution on that ground: s 5J(2).

DIN19 v Minister for Immigration & Anor

2 Feb 2021FCCA[2021] FCCA 1Migration: court challengeMigration
The applicant sought judicial review of an Immigration Assessment Authority decision refusing a protection visa on the basis of claimed fears of harm in Sri Lanka. The Federal Circuit Court found jurisdictional error because the Authority failed to consider whether the PTA was suspended, failed to obtain updated country information, and the Secretary failed to send relevant material about the applicant's brother's protection grant. The decision was quashed and the matter remitted for redetermination.

13 Nov 2019High Court of Australia[2019] HCA 44Migration: court challengeMigration
The plaintiff sought judicial review in the High Court of a Federal Circuit Court decision refusing an extension of time under s 477(2) of the Migration Act and dismissing his judicial review application. The High Court held that the Federal Circuit Court had jurisdiction to dismiss the application, and that its refusal of the extension was based on a permissible threshold assessment of merit, not a full merits review. The application was dismissed.

October 2019 (1)

BVD17 v Minister for Immigration and Border Protection

9 Oct 2019High Court of Australia[2019] HCA 34Migration: court challengeMigration
The appellant sought a protection visa, which a delegate refused. On review by the Immigration Assessment Authority, the Secretary notified the Authority that s 473GB of the Migration Act applied to certain documents and information, but neither the documents nor the fact of notification were disclosed to the appellant. The High Court held that the Authority was not obliged by procedural fairness to disclose the fact of the notification or the documents, and dismissed the appeal.

June 2019 (3)

AWI16 v Minister for Immigration, Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs

25 Jun 2019High Court of Australia[2019] HCA 43Migration: court challengeMigration
The plaintiff sought constitutional or other writ relief against the Minister, Secretary and a departmental officer concerning the handling of his requests for ministerial intervention under ss 48B and 417 of the Migration Act. The requests had been finalised by departmental officers without referral to the Minister because they did not meet departmental guidelines. The High Court held the application disclosed no arguable basis for relief and dismissed it with costs.

Plaintiff S53-2019 v Minister for Immigration, Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs

25 Jun 2019High Court of Australia[2019] HCA 42Migration: court challengeMigration
The plaintiff, a Sri Lankan citizen whose protection visa application had been refused, requested the Minister intervene under s48B or s417 of the Migration Act. A departmental officer finalised the s48B request without referral to the Minister. The High Court dismissed the application, holding there was no delegation, the exercise of non-statutory executive power was not beyond power, and the consideration of such requests is not conditioned by procedural fairness.

M47/2018 v Minister for Home Affairs

12 Jun 2019High Court of Australia[2019] HCA 17Migration: court challengeMigration
The plaintiff, an unlawful non-citizen held in immigration detention, brought a special case to the High Court challenging whether ss 189 and 196 of the Migration Act authorised his continued detention and whether those provisions were beyond Commonwealth legislative power. The Court found that because the plaintiff had deliberately withheld information about his identity and nationality, it was impossible to conclude that there was no real prospect of his removal, so the questions reserved did not arise and no relief was granted.

February 2019 (1)

Minister for Immigration and Border Protection v SZMTA; CQZ15 v Minister for Immigration and Border Protection; BEG15 v Minister for Immigration and Border Protection

13 Feb 2019High Court of Australia[2019] HCA 3Migration: court challengeMigration
The High Court allowed the Minister's appeal in SZMTA, holding that a breach of s424A of the Migration Act does not automatically amount to jurisdictional error; instead, the breach must be material, meaning it could have affected the outcome. The Court dismissed the appeals in CQZ15 and BEG15, finding that failures to comply with procedural fairness obligations did not constitute jurisdictional error because they did not result in practical injustice.

November 2018 (1)

Wehbe v Minister for Home Affairs

7 Nov 2018High Court of Australia[2018] HCA 50Migration: court challengeVisa integrityMigration
The plaintiff sought judicial review of a delegate's decision refusing her partner visa application on the basis that she had provided a bogus marriage certificate, alleging that her migration agent's erroneous email amounted to fraud and jurisdictional error. The High Court held that the agent's mistake was not fraudulent, and that even if it were, it was not material because the delegate's decision would inevitably have been the same given the marriage certificate was a bogus document.

16 Nov 2000High Court of Australia[2000] HCA 57Migration: court challengeMigration
The prosecutor, a refugee applicant, sought constitutional writs against the Refugee Review Tribunal, arguing he was denied procedural fairness because the Tribunal relied on credibility matters without giving him a chance to respond. The High Court held that a denial of procedural fairness amounting to a jurisdictional error entitled the prosecutor to relief, even without proof of a possible successful outcome. Orders absolute were made for prohibition, certiorari and mandamus.

October 2000 (1)

Minister for Immigration v Haji Ibrahim

26 Oct 2000High Court of Australia[2000] HCA 55Migration: court challengeMigration
The High Court of Australia dealt with the interpretation of the Refugees Convention definition in the context of clan-based civil conflict in Somalia. The Court considered whether the Convention definition permits or requires examination of the motivation or objects of a civil war, or demonstration of differential operation upon an applicant's social group. The appeal by the Minister was allowed and the Full Federal Court's orders were set aside, with the appeal to that court dismissed.

Chen Shi Hai v Minister for Immigration and Multicultural Affairs

13 Apr 2000High Court of Australia[2000] HCA 19Migration: court challengeMigration
The appellant, an infant 'black child' born in China in breach of the one child policy, sought a protection visa on the basis that he would face serious disadvantage amounting to persecution. The Refugee Review Tribunal found he would suffer such harm but held 'black children' were not a particular social group, and the Full Federal Court agreed. The High Court allowed the appeal, holding that 'black children' can constitute a particular social group and that the feared harm was persecution for a Convention reason.

The prosecutor sought prerogative relief in the High Court against a Refugee Review Tribunal decision refusing him a protection visa, arguing the Tribunal failed to take into account relevant considerations and evidence and that s 430(1) of the Migration Act required it to refer to contrary evidence. June 1997 (1)

Minister for Immigration & Ethnic Affairs v Guo Wei Rong

13 Jun 1997High Court of Australia[1997] HCA 22Migration: court challengeMigration
The High Court allowed the Minister's appeals, holding that the Full Court of the Federal Court erred in finding that the Refugee Review Tribunal had misapplied the 'real chance' test for a well-founded fear of persecution. The Court clarified that a fear of persecution is well-founded if there is a real chance of persecution occurring, and that the Tribunal's findings were open to it. The matter was remitted with the first respondents' appeals dismissed.

October 1994 (1)

Cunliffe v Commonwealth ("Migration Agents case")

12 Oct 1994High Court of Australia[1994] HCA 44Migration: court challengeMigration
The High Court considered a challenge to Part 2A of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth), which requires persons giving immigration assistance to be registered. The plaintiffs argued that the Part was beyond the Commonwealth's legislative power and infringed the implied freedom of political communication and s 92 of the Constitution. The Court held that Part 2A is wholly valid under the aliens power, does not infringe the implied freedom, and any burden on interstate intercourse is proportionate to a legitimate aim.

Chu Kheng Lim v Minister for Immigration Local Government & Ethnic Affairs

8 Dec 1992High Court of Australia[1992] HCA 64Migration: court challengeMigration
The plaintiffs, Cambodian nationals who arrived in Australia by boat, challenged the validity of provisions in the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) that mandated their detention pending removal or grant of an entry permit, and that limited the courts' power to order their release. The High Court held that the detention provisions (ss 54L and 54N) were valid as they were non-punitive and within the aliens power, but that s 54R was invalid because it usurped judicial power by preventing courts from ordering the release of unlawfully detained persons.
